unit.can_do_en: say who is in my family.

judge.reason: Same question: is your family in Brazil; only register differs.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Mun vanhemmat ja veli asuu siel.
lines.text_kirja: Minun vanhempani ja veljeni asuvat siellä.
lines.gloss_en: My parents and brother live there.

judge.reason: Parents and brother live there in both; spoken uses colloquial verb agreement.

puhe.text: Mun vanhemmat ja veli asuu siel.

kirja.text: Minun vanhempani ja veljeni asuvat siellä.

judge.reason: Both ask whether you miss them; 'niitä' vs 'heitä' is register.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Joo, tosi paljon. Me soitetaan joka sunnuntai.
lines.text_kirja: Kyllä, todella paljon. Me soitamme joka sunnuntai.
lines.gloss_en: Yes, very much. We call every Sunday.

judge.reason: Yes, very much; we call every Sunday in both; spoken passive 'soitetaan' means 'we call'.

puhe.text: Joo, tosi paljon. Me soitetaan joka sunnuntai.

kirja.text: Kyllä, todella paljon. Me soitamme joka sunnuntai.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.gloss_en: Will they come and visit Finland?

judge.reason: Both ask whether they come to visit Finland.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Joo, kesällä! Mun äiti haluu nähä lunta.
lines.text_kirja: Kyllä, kesällä! Minun äitini haluaa nähdä lunta.
lines.gloss_en: Yes, in the summer! My mother wants to see snow.

judge.reason: Yes, in summer; my mother wants to see snow in both.

puhe.text: Joo, kesällä! Mun äiti haluu nähä lunta.

kirja.text: Kyllä, kesällä! Minun äitini haluaa nähdä lunta.

lines.speaker: Aino
lines.gloss_en: Then they need to come in winter!

judge.reason: Both say they must then come in winter; 'niitten' vs 'heidän' is register.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: On with -ko to ask a question. Speech often says -ks: onks.
Sinä with -n for 'your': sinun. Speech shortens it to sun.

forms.form_name_en: nominative singular, with the possessive ending for your
forms.why_en: Books add -si for 'your', with an extra e: perheesi. Speech drops it and says sun perhe.
Minä with -n: minun pitää means I have to. Speech shortens it to mun.

forms.form_name_en: nominative plural, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: Vanhempi, parent. Many plus 'my': vanhempani. Speech says mun vanhemmat and drops -ni.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.

forms.form_name_en: nominative singular, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: Books add -ni for 'my': veljeni, with lj in place of l. Speech drops it and says mun veli.
Books add -vat for 'they': asuvat. Speech uses the he or she form: ne asuu.
Siellä means there. Speech shortens -llä to -l: Siellä becomes Siel.
Sinä with -lla. With on it means 'you have'. Speech shortens it to sul.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person plural, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Tulevat (they come) with the question ending -ko: tulevatko. Speech says tuleeks ne.

forms.lemma_meaning_en: to visit, to go, to be OK
forms.why_en: Käydä takes -mään after tulla (to come): tulla käymään means 'to come and visit'.
Adds -llä to kesä to say when: kesällä, 'in the summer'.

forms.form_name_en: nominative singular, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: Books add -ni for 'my': äitini. Speech drops it and says mun äiti.
Books write haluaa. Speech turns aa into uu: haluu.
Speech drops the d: nähdä becomes nähä. Books write nähdä.
Lumi becomes lunta for some snow: m changes to n and -ta is added.
Speech shortens sitten to sit. Books write sitten.
Books write heidän pitää. Speech uses niitten, from ne. Pitää (must) wants this form of the person.
